My mother quit her Mounjaro® at 64. She died at 67. Three years of regained weight, climbing A1C, atrial fibrillation, and a stroke that should have been preventable.

When I asked her cardiologist how that was possible — given that her bloodwork the year before she quit had been the best of her life — what he told me changed everything I thought I knew about GLP-1 side effects.

Because three weeks ago, I was standing in the same place my mother stood. Same medication class. Same side effects. Same GP about to tell me to discontinue. And I almost did exactly what my mother did, without asking the one question that would have saved her life.

My constipation had hit every 5-6 days. The sulfur burps had me canceling lunches. The 3 PM fatigue felt like someone had pulled a plug. And a flutter at the top of my stairs had started about a month before my next GP appointment.

My GP didn't hesitate.

"You're tolerating the medication poorly. Some patients do. Let's talk about discontinuing the Wegovy® and going back to metformin. We can revisit when the GI side effects calm down."

Eight minutes. That's how long the appointment lasted. She heard "constipation, sulfur burps, fatigue, flutter," wrote "medication intolerance" on the chart, and told me to come back in three months to discuss next steps.

But my husband Tom works in healthcare administration. He wouldn't let it go.

"Your GP is treating your symptoms," he said. "A functional medicine specialist treats what's causing your symptoms. Those are two different things. Before you stop a medication that's been working for your A1C, I want someone looking at what's actually happening inside."

He made the appointment for me with Dr. Lara Chen, a functional medicine internist at the integrative health clinic on Lake Avenue in Boise.

She spent an hour with me. Not eight minutes.

She ran tests my regular GP had never ordered. Intracellular magnesium. Methylmalonic acid — the actual B12 marker that catches tissue depletion before serum drops. Comprehensive electrolyte panel. Heart rate variability. A brief echo to check left atrial size. A rhythm strip I sat for in her office.

She checked things my GP had never checked in eleven years of appointments.

When she came back with the results, she wasn't smiling.

"Your symptoms tell me one thing — the medication is causing GI side effects and you're showing early cardiac signs. That's what your GP is reacting to. But these tests tell me something your symptoms can't."

She turned the monitor toward me. Graphs. Color-coded charts. Tissue magnesium data.

"This is your intracellular magnesium. The magnesium actually inside your cells — your cardiac muscle, your nerve tissue, your gut smooth muscle. Not the magnesium in your bloodstream."

She pointed at a range on the chart.

"A healthy woman your age should be here."

She pointed at another range. Much lower.

"You're here. I normally see this level of tissue depletion in patients who've quit their GLP-1 medications and developed cardiovascular complications six to eighteen months later. You haven't quit yet. Your tissue magnesium collapsed from rapid weight loss alone."

I stared at her. "But my GP said the side effects were the problem. If we stop the Wegovy® —"

"The side effects are the last thing to change," she said. "Your tissue magnesium has been depleting for months — probably since month three on the medication, before your symptoms even started. The constipation, the burps, the flutter — those are not the disease. They're the alarm system telling you the tissue is empty."

She let that settle.

"Think about it. Your sulfur burps didn't start overnight. They crept. The fatigue crept. The flutter is the newest symptom. Your symptoms have been ramping for months. Your GP watched them ramp and said 'tolerating poorly.' But what was happening inside your cells during that time? The depletion was already deep. The symptoms you're describing today are the surface of what's three months ahead of where you actually are."

I felt sick. "So what does stopping the Wegovy® do?"

She was direct.

"Stopping reverses the appetite suppression. You'll start eating normally again. Your weight will come back — most patients regain 60-80% within eighteen months. Your A1C will climb. Your GP will see the numbers reverse and say 'see, the medication was working.' She'll send you back to insulin or metformin."

She paused.

"But the tissue magnesium that depleted during your time on Wegovy® doesn't replete on its own. Your gut bacteria that depleted during reduced eating don't restore from one good meal. Your B12 reserves that dropped during appetite suppression don't snap back. And cardiac muscle that's been running on low magnesium for months — that doesn't bounce back when you start eating more."

"The medication put your weight in range. But the cofactor depletion the medication caused is still there when you stop. Worse, actually — because now you're putting regaining-weight stress on top of the existing deficits."

She looked at me. "That's the trajectory I see in patients who quit. The medication leaves. The damage stays."

And that's when I understood what happened to my mother.

She'd been on Mounjaro® for four years. Started at 60 — for type 2 diabetes that had crept up since menopause. Her endocrinologist called it "a wonder drug for women her age." Said it would normalize her A1C, take off the weight, protect her cardiovascular system.

The first three years were her best years since she was 50. She lost 64 pounds. Her A1C went from 7.8 to 5.5. She had energy. She started hiking again — her favorite activity that diabetes fatigue had taken from her.

She felt twenty years younger.

Then around year three she started complaining about constipation. The sulfur burps. The fatigue she couldn't shake. A "fluttery feeling" she described to my father at the breakfast table.

Her doctor told her what mine told me.

"You're tolerating the medication poorly. Let's discontinue."

My mother trusted her doctor. She'd trusted that doctor for thirty years.

She quit Mounjaro® in August 2022.

By Christmas she'd gained 22 pounds back.

By the next summer she'd gained 51.

By month eighteen, she was 78 pounds heavier than the day she quit. Her A1C was back at 8.3. Her blood pressure was rising. She was exhausted.

I remember her telling me at Thanksgiving that year: "I should have just stayed on it. Whatever it was doing to my gut, it was better than this."

In February 2025, she had a stroke. Right hemispheric. Atrial fibrillation that no one had caught. She was 67.

She survived eleven days in the hospital. She didn't recover speech. She didn't recover the right side of her body. She died of a second cardiac event in the rehab facility three weeks later.

I told Dr. Chen all of this. She was quiet for a long moment.

"That pattern is unfortunately common," she said. "It's recognizable in retrospect. The medication kept her weight in range and her A1C controlled. But the cofactor depletion — particularly the cardiac tissue magnesium — was happening underneath. When she quit, the weight came back, but the magnesium didn't. Then atrial fibrillation became more likely. Then stroke risk increased. Most cardiologists in 2022 weren't looking for the connection because the GLP-1 wave was too new."

There it was. The answer I'd carried since I was 39, standing in a hospital chapel writing my mother's eulogy.

Her A1C was controlled for four years. And she still died of complications the medication was supposed to prevent.

Now a specialist was telling me why.

"So what do I do?" I asked. "Is quitting the only option?"

She said I had two paths.

Path one: stop the Wegovy®. The GI symptoms improve in 4-6 weeks as your appetite returns. Your GP sees you regaining weight and approves the discontinuation. "The medication wasn't right for you."

"But your tissue magnesium stays depleted," she said. "Your A1C climbs over the next twelve months. Your cardiac risk rises. Most patients don't connect what happens next to the period they were on the medication. They blame their own discipline. They start the next round of metformin or insulin. The damage compounds quietly."

Path two: stay on Wegovy®. Address the cofactor depletion the medication is causing. Actually treat the root cause.

"How?" I asked.

She explained:

Your symptoms come from depleted tissue stores. Cardiac muscle, gut smooth muscle, and nerve tissue all rely on magnesium for normal contraction and signaling. When tissue magnesium drops, those tissues stop functioning normally.

Cardiac muscle: premature atrial contractions, then atrial fibrillation if depletion continues. The flutter I was describing.

Gut smooth muscle: motility slows. The slow stomach causes the sulfur burps. The slow intestines cause the constipation.

Nerve tissue: B12 depletion compounds magnesium depletion. The fatigue isn't lack of sleep. It's tissue starvation.

"GLP-1 medications cause rapid weight loss, reduced food intake, and altered gut absorption," she said. "Tissue magnesium, B12, and gut bacteria all collapse fast on these medications. The blood tests look fine because the body protects serum levels last. By the time your blood shows it, the damage has been compounding for months."

"The medication itself is fine. The cofactor depletion is what's causing your symptoms — and what killed your mother."

She said the most effective approach for replenishing tissue magnesium, supporting B12 status, and restoring gut function in GLP-1 patients is the combination of bioavailable magnesium glycinate plus citrate, standardized ginger root extract, and methylcobalamin B12.

I almost laughed. "Magnesium and ginger? My GP wants me to quit the medication and you're telling me about magnesium?"

She pulled up the research. "Your tissue needs specific cofactor support to function during rapid weight loss. Magnesium glycinate at clinical dose absorbs at 95-98% — three times what magnesium oxide does. Standardized ginger root extract at 5% gingerols speeds gastric emptying without fighting the medication. Methylcobalamin B12 bypasses the absorption issues that develop on GLP-1 medications. Together they replete tissue stores within four to six weeks."

"It's the same target the medication needs to work without harming you. The medication is causing the cofactor depletion. You need cofactor replacement that works WITH the medication, not instead of it."

She held up a finger. "But most magnesium supplements are useless for this."

Magnesium oxide. 4% bioavailability. Cheap fillers. The studies use citrate or glycinate. The bottles on Amazon say "high-dose" but contain a tenth of the labeled magnesium in bioavailable form. Most ginger supplements are unstandardized commercial powder with no measurable gingerols. Most B12 is cyanocobalamin — the cheap synthetic that GLP-1 patients can't absorb.

So I started looking. Most were garbage.

First brand — Amazon, the most-reviewed "GLP-1 multivitamin" with 12,000 reviews. Six weeks. Sulfur burps continued. Flutter continued. Checked the label: magnesium oxide, unstandardized ginger powder, cheap cyanocobalamin B12.

Second brand — Whole Foods, the "premium GLP-1 support" supplement. Eight weeks. Constipation marginally better but the flutter was the same. Still magnesium oxide. Still no real ginger.

Third brand — the supplement store on Mountain Avenue, the most expensive bottle on the shelf. Four weeks. No real change.

I was running out of time. My follow-up with my GP was three weeks away. She was going to ask if I'd stopped the Wegovy®.

After the third brand failed, I went back to Dr. Chen.

She wasn't surprised. "Most patients try three or four brands before they find a real one. The supplement industry is exploiting GLP-1 patients right now — slapping 'GLP-1' on existing products and tripling the price."

She handed me a small black notebook. "I've tested twelve in lab through a partner. One passed."

She wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad.

GLP-1 SOS™.

"250mg of bioavailable magnesium glycinate plus citrate blend. Not oxide. Not in pill form that doesn't dissolve. 200mg ginger root standardized to 5% gingerols. 500mcg methylcobalamin B12 — the active form. Manufactured at a single FDA-registered facility in Ruston, Utah. Third-party tested every batch. Certificate of Analysis available on their site."

"$24.99 a month on subscription. Less than the prescription Citrucel your GP would have moved you to. 60-day money-back guarantee. If your symptoms don't improve in 60 days, you send the bottle back and get a full refund. No questions."

I started taking it that night.

Two capsules with dinner. Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing.

Day three, I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. I sat on the edge of the tub for a minute after, because I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

✅ 48 hours after my first dose: I had lunch with my book club. I waited for the sulfur burps. They didn't come.

✅ Week 2: Sleeping through the night. Energy through the afternoon for the first time in months.

✅ Week 3: I went back to Dr. Chen for repeat testing. She compared the panels. Tissue magnesium climbing. Methylmalonic acid trending down. Heart rate variability improving.

✅ Week 4: Climbed my stairs at home carrying laundry. At the top, I waited. The flutter didn't come. I climbed up and down four more times to be sure. No PACs.

✅ Week 5: I went back to my GP for my follow-up.

She asked about the GI side effects. I told her: gone.

She asked about the medication. I told her I was still on it.

She pulled up my chart. Previous visit: medication intolerance, discontinuation recommended.

"You didn't stop the Wegovy®?"

"No. I went to a functional medicine specialist. She tested my tissue magnesium and found significant depletion. I started a magnesium-ginger-B12 formulation she recommended. My symptoms resolved."

Long silence.

"I haven't seen that approach before. But your weight is stable. Your A1C looks great. The flutter you described last visit — has it returned?"

"No."

She wrote a few notes in my chart. "Continue what you're doing. I'd like to see you in three months. Bring the supplement information so I can document it for your file."

I walked out. Sat in my car. Called Tom.

"I stayed on the Wegovy®. My GP approved."

He exhaled. "You did it."

"I did it."

Two weeks later Tom and I hiked the trail my mother used to take me on when I was a kid. Six miles. Up Lake Avenue past the reservoir, out to the overlook where you can see four states on a clear day.

I hadn't done it in two years.

At the overlook I sat on the bench my father had installed in my mother's memory the year before she died. Looked out at the four states. Thought about her.

She had taken me there at twelve. At twenty-five. At thirty-two.

At sixty-two she said she'd lost too much energy to make the climb.

At sixty-four she quit Mounjaro® because of side effects nobody had told her could be solved.

At sixty-seven she had a stroke.

I sat on her bench at the overlook and thought: she didn't have to die.

Dr. Chen told me later that if I'd quit the Wegovy® — managing the symptoms by removing the medication while the tissue depletion continued — I'd be on the same trajectory my mother was on.

"Your mother's story isn't unusual," she said. "It's the standard outcome when patients quit GLP-1 medications because of cofactor depletion symptoms. The medication leaves. The damage stays. The weight comes back. The cardiac risk rises. Eight to twenty-four months later — a stroke or a cardiac event."

My mother quit her Mounjaro® to relieve the symptoms. Her tissue magnesium, her B12, her gut bacteria — they kept declining. Three years later she was gone.

I fixed the cause. Four months later my labs are better than they were the year before my mother quit hers.

If you're reading this, you're where I was.

Your GLP-1 medication is working — your weight is dropping, your A1C is improving. But the side effects have hit. Constipation. Sulfur burps. Fatigue. Maybe a flutter at the top of the stairs.

Your GP wants you to stop. She probably won't say "quit" — she'll say "discontinue" or "consider alternatives" or "let's revisit if things calm down." She'll write it on your chart as "medication intolerance."

You'll feel a small relief that someone is taking your symptoms seriously.

But here's what I wish someone had told me three weeks ago, before I almost did what my mother did:

Your side effects aren't the medication failing. They're the tissue magnesium, B12, and gut bacteria collapsing UNDER the medication. The medication is doing exactly what it's designed to do — controlling your weight and your A1C. But the rapid weight loss, the reduced food intake, the altered absorption — those cause cofactor depletion the medication itself can't address.

Quitting reverses the medication. It does not reverse the depletion.

My mother proved where that path leads.

That's what I did. My GP saw a patient who'd been recommended to discontinue but instead showed up symptom-free, weight stable, A1C optimal. She didn't argue. She didn't push discontinuation. She said "continue what you're doing."

Function doesn't argue.

Don't wait until your GP convinces you to quit. Don't follow the same road my mother followed for the three years before she died.

Last March I found Wegovy® in my sister's bathroom cabinet.

I closed the door the way you'd close it if you'd just opened a letter that wasn't addressed to you. Quiet. Careful. Like I needed time to decide what I'd just seen.

Seeing a weight-loss drug behind her cotton pads felt like being lied to. A small confounding betrayal I'd needed her to be above.

I didn't speak to her for six months.

I'm on the same drug now.

And there's something I need to tell her before the symptom she's been hiding from me gets worse. I think it's already worse.

Let me back up.

My sister is forty-eight. I'm fifty-nine. We've been close in the way only sisters who survived the same childhood can be close. Three kids between us. One divorce survived (mine). Twenty-six years of Sunday dinners at our mother's table before our mother passed in 2022, and another three years of holding the family together at my kitchen table since.

She lives twelve miles from me in Eagle, Idaho. I live in Boise. I see her almost every week. Or I did, until that Saturday.

I was at her house helping wrap her daughter Maddie's tenth birthday gifts. We'd done this every year together since Maddie was born. She needed paper tape. She said it was in the bathroom drawer.

Behind a stack of cotton pads, in a folded CVS prescription bag, the Wegovy® label was visible through the plastic.

I stood there holding that drawer open for a long time. Then I closed it. I wrapped the gifts. I drank the coffee. I left two hours later without mentioning it.

I drove home and I told my husband Mike. Loudly. I told him she'd taken the easy way. I told him our mother would have been disappointed. I told him I thought she was stronger than that. I said the things you say at the kitchen counter when you're trying to make yourself feel better about a judgment you've just passed.

That night I didn't text her. She didn't text me.

Six months is a long time to not speak to your sister.

In April I missed my niece's birthday party. I lied to Mike about a migraine and stayed home.

In May our grandkids were on the same Little League team and I made sure I arrived after the first inning so we'd be sitting on opposite sides of the field.

In June I drafted a text four times and deleted it four times.

In July I unfollowed her on Instagram so I'd stop checking it.

In August I checked it anyway, on Mike's phone, while he was in the shower.

She'd lost more weight.

I ate the feeling for the rest of the month and into September.

In September my endocrinologist told me my A1C had climbed to 6.4.

She said, in plain English, that I was a year from an insulin pump if nothing changed.

She reminded me my mother had gone the insulin route at 52, and that I was already seven years past that.

She said the word Ozempic. She said Wegovy.

She said: "You have options your mother didn't have."

I drove home and I sat in the driveway for forty-five minutes before I went inside.

I thought about my sister.

I thought about what I'd said about her in my own kitchen seven months earlier.

I thought about my face in the bathroom mirror that night, saying "the real way."

I filled the Wegovy® prescription on a Monday.

I hid it in the glove compartment of my car until the Idaho afternoon sun moved off the windshield, because I didn't want it warming up in there. Then I brought it inside and put it in the back of the fridge.

I put it behind a jar of pickles Mike would never touch.

Then I stood in front of the open refrigerator for a long time looking at the pickle jar.

I had become the exact thing I had walked out of her bathroom for.

Same drug. Same shelf. Same jar.

I closed the fridge.

I lost 51 pounds in the next eight months.

I didn't tell anyone. Not Mike. Not my daughter Jenny in Portland. Not my son Tyler who lives ten minutes away. Especially not Diane.

I was coasting on the lie for a while.

I could take the drug and not have the conversation.

I could be a hypocrite in private.

Then at month three, I went six days without going to the bathroom.

Not painful at first. Just a slow, building bloat. I bought a tub of Metamucil at Albertsons and put it on the counter so Mike would think I was just being responsible about fiber.

Then the burps started.

You know the ones. The rotten-egg taste at the back of your throat. The kind that make the woman next to you on the elliptical at Boise Athletic Club move two machines down.

I cancelled book club. I cancelled lunch with my friend Karen. I told them I had a sinus thing.

By the end of month four I was waking up at three in the morning every single night.

Bone-on-bone burning low in my abdomen. Cramping that wouldn't move. I'd get up, go downstairs, take a Tylenol, sit at the kitchen table waiting for it to take the edge off, and stare at the back of the fridge where the Wegovy pen sat behind the pickle jar.

I never told Mike.

Because the day I told him out loud was the day I'd have to choose between the drug that was finally getting my A1C in range and admitting I'd hidden it from him for ten months.

I went to my GP at month four and a half.

She ran a panel. Iron, ferritin, magnesium, thyroid, B12, protein.

Everything came back normal.

"This is just how some people respond to rapid weight loss," she said. "Increase your fiber. Add a daily Miralax. Take a magnesium tablet at bedtime if it gets bad. It's going to settle. Give it three to six months."

I did exactly what she said.

Week 1-4: Metamucil twice a day. Choked down the wet cardboard. Result: marginal first week, plateau.

Week 5-8: Switched to Miralax every morning. Result: 30% better, then back to baseline.

Week 9-12: My GP wrote me a prescription for Citrucel. $94 for a 60-day supply.

No different than Miralax. I was now spending $94 every two months on what was essentially expensive fiber.

Week 13-16: Amazon "GLP-1 multivitamin" that promised "complete gut support." $42 with overnight Prime.

Marginal first week. Plateau by week three.

I spent over $360 in four months on supplements and prescription fiber and stomach acid blockers because the Tylenol I was taking every night had burned a hole in my stomach lining.

I still hadn't gone normally in five months.

And I was starting to notice something else.

Sometimes at the top of the stairs I'd feel a little flutter in my chest. Not pain. Not enough to mention. Just enough to make me stop and put my hand on the bannister for a second before I kept going.

I told myself it was the stairs. I was 59. The stairs were going to get harder.

Then my friend Karen called me in February and told me her sister-in-law's cardiologist had found atrial fibrillation in a woman who'd lost 60 pounds on Mounjaro® in nine months.

"Karen," I said. "What does atrial fibrillation feel like?"

"Sometimes nothing," she said. "Sometimes a little flutter in your chest at the top of the stairs."

I sat down on my couch and didn't say anything for a long time.

The next morning I made an appointment with my GP for a referral.

Six-week wait for cardiology.

While I waited, I went to refill my Wegovy® at the independent pharmacy on Bannock Street in downtown Boise. Coleman Pharmacy. I'd been going there for four years — small, two-pharmacist shop, owned by a woman named Dr. Sarah Coleman who'd been a hospital pharmacist at St. Luke's Boise for thirty-one years before opening her own place.

She knew my whole medication history. She knew my A1C numbers. She knew my mother had been her patient at St. Luke's.

When she handed me my prescription, she asked the question my GP never asked.

"How are you actually feeling, Carol?"

I told her. The bowel movements. The burps. The Tylenol. The Amazon multivitamin. The fluttering at the top of the stairs.

She set the prescription bag down very slowly on the counter and looked at me.

"Carol. Come to the back."

She walked me to a small consultation room where she did her medication-therapy reviews. Sat me down at a table. Then she opened a binder and turned to a page near the front.

"Can I tell you something I learned in thirty-one years filling prescriptions for every medication you can name?"

I nodded.

"Your GP told you the truth about your symptoms. But she told you only half of it. There's not one problem happening here. There are two. And almost no GP is addressing the second one because it doesn't show up in standard labs."

"I had standard labs. They were normal."

"I know. They almost always are."

She slid the binder across the table to me.

"Your medication — Wegovy®, Ozempic®, Mounjaro® — they slow gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That's the therapeutic effect. It's why your A1C dropped. It's also why food sits in your stomach long enough to start fermenting. Those are the sulfur burps. And it's why your intestinal motility slowed, which is the constipation. Your GP is treating those symptoms. She's not wrong about them. They're real, and with the right protocol they resolve."

"Okay."

"But here's what almost nobody is telling women on GLP-1s. While you've been losing weight, your body has been depleting its magnesium stores at three times the normal rate. Rapid fat loss triggers it. Reduced food intake compounds it. And the magnesium that goes first is the magnesium your body considers most disposable — which is not, unfortunately, the magnesium in your blood. It's the magnesium in your tissues. Your cardiac muscle. Your nerve endings. Your bone."

"But my magnesium test was normal."

"Carol. Less than one percent of your body's magnesium is in your blood. The blood test tells you what's in the bloodstream right now. It tells you almost nothing about what's in your heart muscle. Or your nerves. Or your bones. The body protects serum magnesium last and hardest, because if blood magnesium crashes, you die. So it strips the tissues first. The blood looks fine for months while the tissues quietly empty out."

I thought about the flutter at the top of the stairs.

She kept going.

"Magnesium is the cofactor for over six hundred enzymatic processes in your body. The two most magnesium-dependent tissues you have are your cardiac muscle and your neural tissue. When you deplete tissue magnesium fast — and a GLP-1 patient losing weight is depleting it fast — the cardiac muscle starts having trouble relaxing properly between contractions. That's how atrial fibrillation begins. Quietly. Intermittently. Before anyone catches it on an EKG."

"That's what's happening when I feel the flutter."

"I would bet on it. And here's the worst part. The fiber and the Miralax your GP gave you — those don't address it. The Amazon multivitamin you tried — that doesn't address it either. Most generic magnesium tablets are magnesium oxide, which your gut barely absorbs. The magnesium that actually reaches the tissue has to be a bioavailable form — citrate, glycinate, or a combination — at a therapeutic dose, paired with something that addresses the gastric emptying side."

"Why has nobody told me this?"

"Because the supplement industry has spent thirty years selling fiber to constipated people. The GLP-1 wave is brand new. Most companies are slapping 'GLP-1 SUPPORT' on existing multivitamin labels and charging double for the same thing they were selling in 2019. Ninety percent of what's on Amazon under that label is under-dosed magnesium with no real ginger and no thought to the actual mechanism."

"You've tested them?"

"Last year I sent fifteen of the most popular GLP-1-positioned supplements on Amazon to a third-party lab in Seattle. We did blind assays."

She turned the page in the binder.

"Brand A — labeled 250mg magnesium glycinate — actually contained 23mg of magnesium per dose. Ninety percent under-dosed."

"Brand B — labeled 200mg ginger root extract — was unstandardized commercial powder. No measurable gingerols. Useless."

"Brand C — labeled 500mg magnesium citrate — was magnesium oxide, which your body absorbs maybe 4% of."

"Brand D was contaminated with heavy metals at levels above the FDA's CFR-111 limits."

She paused.

"Exactly one product passed the assay. Magnesium delivered as labeled, in bioavailable citrate-glycinate form. Ginger root standardized to 5% gingerols. Methylcobalamin B12, not the cheap cyanocobalamin synthetic. Manufactured in a single FDA-registered facility in Ruston, Utah. Third-party tested every batch. No fillers."

She wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy® and went through what you're going through. She found a formulator who actually understood the dual mechanism. I recommend it to every GLP-1 patient who walks into this pharmacy now. I have no business relationship with the company. I just don't want to keep watching women like you end up in cardiology waiting rooms for something that was preventable."

I looked at the prescription pad. GLP-1 SOS™.

"And this fixes both problems?"

"If you start now, before the cardiac symptoms become a confirmed diagnosis — yes. Two capsules with dinner. Magnesium pulls water into your gut gently overnight and reaches the depleted tissue including the cardiac muscle. Ginger speeds gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation. B12 rebuilds the nerve and energy reserves. You should see regularity in three days. Sulfur burps usually resolve in 48 hours. The fluttering — if it really is early magnesium depletion — should settle within four to six weeks as the tissue stores rebuild."

"What about my cardiology appointment?"

"Keep it. Tell the cardiologist exactly what we just discussed. Ask her about intracellular magnesium testing if she's seeing rhythm signals. But start the supplement tonight, not after the appointment. Every week you wait is a week the tissue keeps depleting."

"How much is it?"

"$24.99 a month on subscription. Less than what you're already spending on Citrucel and Tylenol and the stomach acid blocker for the lining damage the Tylenol caused. And it has a 60-day money-back guarantee. If it doesn't work for you, you get every dollar back, no return required."

I ordered it from the parking lot.

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. I started to wonder if Dr. Coleman was wrong.

Day three, I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. Just normal. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward for a minute because I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

✅ Week 2: I slept through the night without cramping. Eight hours straight for the first time since September.

✅ Week 3: I had energy at 3 PM. I weeded the entire front yard. I hadn't done that since the spring.

✅ Week 5: I climbed the stairs at home and at the top, I waited. The flutter didn't come.

✅ Week 8: My A1C check came back at 5.7. Not 6.4. Not 5.9. Five point seven. My endocrinologist asked what I'd changed. I told her. She wrote it down.

Then I went to my cardiology appointment.

Saint Alphonsus on West Emerald.

I'd been doing fine for six weeks but I kept the appointment because Dr. Coleman had said to.

The cardiology waiting room is on the second floor. Soft fluorescent lighting. Vinyl chairs. People magazine. Botanical prints on the walls. I checked in and sat down with a clipboard.

Four chairs to my left, on the opposite side of the same row, was my sister.

Diane.

She was wearing an oversized cream cardigan that hung off her shoulders. She'd lost more weight since August — I could see it now even through the sweater. Her hair was in a low loose ponytail. She had a glucose monitor in her open canvas tote on the chair beside her, showing a reading I couldn't make out.

The cardigan was hiding loose skin under her arms. I knew that cardigan. She'd bought it the year our mother died because she needed something soft to wear to the visitation. She'd worn it almost every day for a month after.

She didn't see me.

I sat there with my clipboard in my lap for a long time without filling it out. I watched her.

She was staring at her hands.

She had her right hand pressed lightly against her sternum, the way you do when you're not in pain but you're waiting for the not-pain to turn into pain.

I knew that gesture. I'd been doing it on the stairs for five months.

Diane had been doing it longer.

She hadn't told me. We hadn't been speaking.

She hadn't told anyone, I would guess. Her husband John. Her son Tyler in college. Nobody.

Because the day she said it out loud was the day she'd have to admit, to the people she loved, that the drug she'd been hiding behind cotton pads was the same drug that had brought her to a cardiology waiting room on a Tuesday in February.

I almost got up. I almost crossed the four chairs. I almost said her name.

Then the receptionist called me. "Carol Hendricks?"

I stood up. I picked up my clipboard. I walked past her row. She still didn't look up.

I went into my appointment.

The cardiologist examined me, listened to my heart for a long time, ran the EKG. Then she sat across from me at her little desk and said: "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it. Your rhythm is fine. You're going to be fine."

I left her office. I walked back through the waiting room.

The chair where Diane had been sitting was empty.

I drove home, opened my laptop, and started writing.

"You're tolerating the medication poorly. Some patients do. Let's talk about discontinuing the Wegovy® and going back to metformin. We can revisit when the GI side effects calm down."

Eight minutes. That's how long the appointment lasted. She heard "constipation, sulfur burps, fatigue, flutter," wrote "medication intolerance" on the chart, and told me to come back in three months to discuss next steps.

But my husband Tom works in healthcare administration. He wouldn't let it go.

"Your GP is treating your symptoms," he said. "A functional medicine specialist treats what's causing your symptoms. Those are two different things. Before you stop a medication that's been working for your A1C, I want someone looking at what's actually happening inside."

He made the appointment for me with Dr. Lara Chen, a functional medicine internist at the integrative health clinic on Lake Avenue in Boise.

She spent an hour with me. Not eight minutes.

She ran tests my regular GP had never ordered. Intracellular magnesium. Methylmalonic acid — the actual B12 marker that catches tissue depletion before serum drops. Comprehensive electrolyte panel. Heart rate variability. A brief echo to check left atrial size. A rhythm strip I sat for in her office.

She checked things my GP had never checked in eleven years of appointments.

When she came back with the results, she wasn't smiling.

"Your symptoms tell me one thing — the medication is causing GI side effects and you're showing early cardiac signs. That's what your GP is reacting to. But these tests tell me something your symptoms can't."

She turned the monitor toward me. Graphs. Color-coded charts. Tissue magnesium data.

"This is your intracellular magnesium. The magnesium actually inside your cells — your cardiac muscle, your nerve tissue, your gut smooth muscle. Not the magnesium in your bloodstream."

She pointed at a range on the chart.

"A healthy woman your age should be here."

She pointed at another range. Much lower.

"You're here. I normally see this level of tissue depletion in patients who've quit their GLP-1 medications and developed cardiovascular complications six to eighteen months later. You haven't quit yet. Your tissue magnesium collapsed from rapid weight loss alone."

I stared at her. "But my GP said the side effects were the problem. If we stop the Wegovy® —"

"The side effects are the last thing to change," she said. "Your tissue magnesium has been depleting for months — probably since month three on the medication, before your symptoms even started. The constipation, the burps, the flutter — those are not the disease. They're the alarm system telling you the tissue is empty."

She let that settle.

"Think about it. Your sulfur burps didn't start overnight. They crept. The fatigue crept. The flutter is the newest symptom. Your symptoms have been ramping for months. Your GP watched them ramp and said 'tolerating poorly.' But what was happening inside your cells during that time? The depletion was already deep. The symptoms you're describing today are the surface of what's three months ahead of where you actually are."

I felt sick. "So what does stopping the Wegovy® do?"

She was direct.

"Stopping reverses the appetite suppression. You'll start eating normally again. Your weight will come back — most patients regain 60-80% within eighteen months. Your A1C will climb. Your GP will see the numbers reverse and say 'see, the medication was working.' She'll send you back to insulin or metformin."

She paused.

"But the tissue magnesium that depleted during your time on Wegovy® doesn't replete on its own. Your gut bacteria that depleted during reduced eating don't restore from one good meal. Your B12 reserves that dropped during appetite suppression don't snap back. And cardiac muscle that's been running on low magnesium for months — that doesn't bounce back when you start eating more."

"The medication put your weight in range. But the cofactor depletion the medication caused is still there when you stop. Worse, actually — because now you're putting regaining-weight stress on top of the existing deficits."

She looked at me. "That's the trajectory I see in patients who quit. The medication leaves. The damage stays."

And that's when I understood what happened to my mother.

She'd been on Mounjaro® for four years. Started at 60 — for type 2 diabetes that had crept up since menopause. Her endocrinologist called it "a wonder drug for women her age." Said it would normalize her A1C, take off the weight, protect her cardiovascular system.

The first three years were her best years since she was 50. She lost 64 pounds. Her A1C went from 7.8 to 5.5. She had energy. She started hiking again — her favorite activity that diabetes fatigue had taken from her.

She felt twenty years younger.

Then around year three she started complaining about constipation. The sulfur burps. The fatigue she couldn't shake. A "fluttery feeling" she described to my father at the breakfast table.

Her doctor told her what mine told me.

"You're tolerating the medication poorly. Let's discontinue."

My mother trusted her doctor. She'd trusted that doctor for thirty years.

She quit Mounjaro® in August 2022.

By Christmas she'd gained 22 pounds back.

By the next summer she'd gained 51.

By month eighteen, she was 78 pounds heavier than the day she quit. Her A1C was back at 8.3. Her blood pressure was rising. She was exhausted.

I remember her telling me at Thanksgiving that year: "I should have just stayed on it. Whatever it was doing to my gut, it was better than this."

In February 2025, she had a stroke. Right hemispheric. Atrial fibrillation that no one had caught. She was 67.

She survived eleven days in the hospital. She didn't recover speech. She didn't recover the right side of her body. She died of a second cardiac event in the rehab facility three weeks later.

I told Dr. Chen all of this. She was quiet for a long moment.

"That pattern is unfortunately common," she said. "It's recognizable in retrospect. The medication kept her weight in range and her A1C controlled. But the cofactor depletion — particularly the cardiac tissue magnesium — was happening underneath. When she quit, the weight came back, but the magnesium didn't. Then atrial fibrillation became more likely. Then stroke risk increased. Most cardiologists in 2022 weren't looking for the connection because the GLP-1 wave was too new."

There it was. The answer I'd carried since I was 39, standing in a hospital chapel writing my mother's eulogy.

Her A1C was controlled for four years. And she still died of complications the medication was supposed to prevent.

Now a specialist was telling me why.

"So what do I do?" I asked. "Is quitting the only option?"

She said I had two paths.

Path one: stop the Wegovy®. The GI symptoms improve in 4-6 weeks as your appetite returns. Your GP sees you regaining weight and approves the discontinuation. "The medication wasn't right for you."

"But your tissue magnesium stays depleted," she said. "Your A1C climbs over the next twelve months. Your cardiac risk rises. Most patients don't connect what happens next to the period they were on the medication. They blame their own discipline. They start the next round of metformin or insulin. The damage compounds quietly."

Path two: stay on Wegovy®. Address the cofactor depletion the medication is causing. Actually treat the root cause.

"How?" I asked.

She explained:

Your symptoms come from depleted tissue stores. Cardiac muscle, gut smooth muscle, and nerve tissue all rely on magnesium for normal contraction and signaling. When tissue magnesium drops, those tissues stop functioning normally.

Cardiac muscle: premature atrial contractions, then atrial fibrillation if depletion continues. The flutter I was describing.

Gut smooth muscle: motility slows. The slow stomach causes the sulfur burps. The slow intestines cause the constipation.

Nerve tissue: B12 depletion compounds magnesium depletion. The fatigue isn't lack of sleep. It's tissue starvation.

"GLP-1 medications cause rapid weight loss, reduced food intake, and altered gut absorption," she said. "Tissue magnesium, B12, and gut bacteria all collapse fast on these medications. The blood tests look fine because the body protects serum levels last. By the time your blood shows it, the damage has been compounding for months."

"The medication itself is fine. The cofactor depletion is what's causing your symptoms — and what killed your mother."

She said the most effective approach for replenishing tissue magnesium, supporting B12 status, and restoring gut function in GLP-1 patients is the combination of bioavailable magnesium glycinate plus citrate, standardized ginger root extract, and methylcobalamin B12.

I almost laughed. "Magnesium and ginger? My GP wants me to quit the medication and you're telling me about magnesium?"

She pulled up the research. "Your tissue needs specific cofactor support to function during rapid weight loss. Magnesium glycinate at clinical dose absorbs at 95-98% — three times what magnesium oxide does. Standardized ginger root extract at 5% gingerols speeds gastric emptying without fighting the medication. Methylcobalamin B12 bypasses the absorption issues that develop on GLP-1 medications. Together they replete tissue stores within four to six weeks."

"It's the same target the medication needs to work without harming you. The medication is causing the cofactor depletion. You need cofactor replacement that works WITH the medication, not instead of it."

She held up a finger. "But most magnesium supplements are useless for this."

Magnesium oxide. 4% bioavailability. Cheap fillers. The studies use citrate or glycinate. The bottles on Amazon say "high-dose" but contain a tenth of the labeled magnesium in bioavailable form. Most ginger supplements are unstandardized commercial powder with no measurable gingerols. Most B12 is cyanocobalamin — the cheap synthetic that GLP-1 patients can't absorb.

So I started looking. Most were garbage.

First brand — Amazon, the most-reviewed "GLP-1 multivitamin" with 12,000 reviews. Six weeks. Sulfur burps continued. Flutter continued. Checked the label: magnesium oxide, unstandardized ginger powder, cheap cyanocobalamin B12.

Second brand — Whole Foods, the "premium GLP-1 support" supplement. Eight weeks. Constipation marginally better but the flutter was the same. Still magnesium oxide. Still no real ginger.

Third brand — the supplement store on Mountain Avenue, the most expensive bottle on the shelf. Four weeks. No real change.

I was running out of time. My follow-up with my GP was three weeks away. She was going to ask if I'd stopped the Wegovy®.

After the third brand failed, I went back to Dr. Chen.

She wasn't surprised. "Most patients try three or four brands before they find a real one. The supplement industry is exploiting GLP-1 patients right now — slapping 'GLP-1' on existing products and tripling the price."

She handed me a small black notebook. "I've tested twelve in lab through a partner. One passed."

She wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad.

GLP-1 SOS™.

"250mg of bioavailable magnesium glycinate plus citrate blend. Not oxide. Not in pill form that doesn't dissolve. 200mg ginger root standardized to 5% gingerols. 500mcg methylcobalamin B12 — the active form. Manufactured at a single FDA-registered facility in Ruston, Utah. Third-party tested every batch. Certificate of Analysis available on their site."

"$24.99 a month on subscription. Less than the prescription Citrucel your GP would have moved you to. 60-day money-back guarantee. If your symptoms don't improve in 60 days, you send the bottle back and get a full refund. No questions."

I started taking it that night.

Two capsules with dinner. Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing.

Day three, I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. I sat on the edge of the tub for a minute after, because I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

✅ 48 hours after my first dose: I had lunch with my book club. I waited for the sulfur burps. They didn't come.

✅ Week 2: Sleeping through the night. Energy through the afternoon for the first time in months.

✅ Week 3: I went back to Dr. Chen for repeat testing. She compared the panels. Tissue magnesium climbing. Methylmalonic acid trending down. Heart rate variability improving.

✅ Week 4: Climbed my stairs at home carrying laundry. At the top, I waited. The flutter didn't come. I climbed up and down four more times to be sure. No PACs.

✅ Week 5: I went back to my GP for my follow-up.

She asked about the GI side effects. I told her: gone.

She asked about the medication. I told her I was still on it.

She pulled up my chart. Previous visit: medication intolerance, discontinuation recommended.

"You didn't stop the Wegovy®?"

"No. I went to a functional medicine specialist. She tested my tissue magnesium and found significant depletion. I started a magnesium-ginger-B12 formulation she recommended. My symptoms resolved."

Long silence.

"I haven't seen that approach before. But your weight is stable. Your A1C looks great. The flutter you described last visit — has it returned?"

"No."

She wrote a few notes in my chart. "Continue what you're doing. I'd like to see you in three months. Bring the supplement information so I can document it for your file."

I walked out. Sat in my car. Called Tom.

"I stayed on the Wegovy®. My GP approved."

He exhaled. "You did it."

"I did it."

Two weeks later Tom and I hiked the trail my mother used to take me on when I was a kid. Six miles. Up Lake Avenue past the reservoir, out to the overlook where you can see four states on a clear day.

I hadn't done it in two years.

At the overlook I sat on the bench my father had installed in my mother's memory the year before she died. Looked out at the four states. Thought about her.

She had taken me there at twelve. At twenty-five. At thirty-two.

At sixty-two she said she'd lost too much energy to make the climb.

At sixty-four she quit Mounjaro® because of side effects nobody had told her could be solved.

At sixty-seven she had a stroke.

I sat on her bench at the overlook and thought: she didn't have to die.

Dr. Chen told me later that if I'd quit the Wegovy® — managing the symptoms by removing the medication while the tissue depletion continued — I'd be on the same trajectory my mother was on.

"Your mother's story isn't unusual," she said. "It's the standard outcome when patients quit GLP-1 medications because of cofactor depletion symptoms. The medication leaves. The damage stays. The weight comes back. The cardiac risk rises. Eight to twenty-four months later — a stroke or a cardiac event."

My mother quit her Mounjaro® to relieve the symptoms. Her tissue magnesium, her B12, her gut bacteria — they kept declining. Three years later she was gone.

I fixed the cause. Four months later my labs are better than they were the year before my mother quit hers.

If you're reading this, you're where I was.

Your GLP-1 medication is working — your weight is dropping, your A1C is improving. But the side effects have hit. Constipation. Sulfur burps. Fatigue. Maybe a flutter at the top of the stairs.

The medication is doing exactly what it's designed to do — controlling your weight and your A1C. But the rapid weight loss, the reduced food intake, the altered absorption — those cause cofactor depletion the medication itself can't address.

If you go once every 3 or 4 days no matter how much water you drink or how much fiber you choke down — and you keep getting told to "just give it time" — I want to tell you what finally made sense of all of it for me.

Because I watched my best friend live it. And once I understood what was actually going on, I'll be honest: I was angry. Not at any one person. Angry that the answer was this simple, and it took us almost two years to find it.

Let me tell you about Gail.

For the better part of two years, my best friend was miserable. Her constipation got so bad she'd go once every five or six days — not "a little backed up," but sitting in the bathroom for 45 minutes, straining, near tears, feeling like her body had simply stopped working.

Her stomach stayed bloated to the point that she looked six months pregnant after every meal. Everything in her closet had to be stretchy or loose, because by 3 PM her waistband was cutting into her.

And the fog. She'd sleep eight hours and wake up feeling like she'd been sedated. She'd lose the end of her own sentences. Her energy was gone by 2 PM every single day. She started to feel like she was going a little crazy, because nobody could tell her what was actually wrong.

It all started a few months after she began her shots.

So she did what you're supposed to do. She saw her doctor. A gastroenterologist. Thousands of dollars in appointments, bloodwork, a colonoscopy, stool tests — the whole nine yards. And every result came back "normal."

And the advice was always the same:

"Your bloodwork looks fine." "It's probably just IBS." "Drink more water." "Eat more fiber." "Have you tried Miralax?"

Here's the thing — none of that advice is wrong, exactly. For a typical gut, it's perfectly reasonable. It just wasn't built for what was actually happening to hers. And that's the part nobody connected for her.

They had her on Miralax, Metamucil, probiotics, magnesium — a rotating door of band-aids. The fiber powders made her more bloated. Months of money, restrictive diets, cutting out gluten and dairy. She couldn't enjoy a meal or leave the house without mapping the bathrooms. And nothing got better. It stayed the same or got worse.

I couldn't stand watching her do everything she was told and keep sinking. So I started reading. Late nights, medical journals, functional-medicine articles. And I finally found the piece no one had ever explained to her.

Here's what nobody tells you: your gut isn't supposed to need to be forced. It moves on its own — in waves. Peristalsis. The muscles squeeze in a rhythm and push everything along. That rhythm is what "regular" actually means. Not a flush. A rhythm.

And a GLP-1 slows that rhythm down. That's literally how the medication works — it slows your stomach so you stay full longer. The full feeling is the whole point. The gut grinding to a crawl is the side effect nobody warns you about.

So once the rhythm has stalled, drinking more water and eating more fiber doesn't fix it. You're just loading more cargo onto a train that isn't moving. And laxatives? They shove water past the stall. None of them restart the rhythm.

It's like a train yard where every car is loaded and ready — but no signal ever goes out to move them. The cars are fine. The track is fine. Nothing leaves the yard.

That's why you can drink gallons of water, eat pounds of fiber, and still go once every four days. The raw materials are all there. The gut just isn't getting the push to move them.

And here's what actually helps a slowed-down gut — and not one of them is a laxative:

Magnesium, the citrate form, draws in a little water gently and relaxes the gut wall. It works with a slow system instead of blasting it.

Ginger — and this is the one almost no one talks about — is a clinically-studied prokinetic. It supports the stomach emptying that a GLP-1 slows down. It works at the source, not just the exit.

The right gut bacteria — a real multi-strain probiotic to support the flora that keep things moving and calm the fermentation behind the bloating and the sulfur burps. (Eating 60% less on a GLP-1 quietly starves them.)

This isn't fringe. Ginger has been studied for gastric motility for years. Magnesium is one of the most-studied minerals there is for regularity. It's just not the one-size advice you get in a ten-minute appointment. It's a different problem, so it needs a different fix.

Gail finally found a functional medicine doctor who actually looked deeper — and told her almost word-for-word what I'd been reading. Her gut had slowed down. Last March I found Wegovy® in my sister's bathroom cabinet.

I closed the door the way you'd close it if you'd just opened a letter that wasn't addressed to you. Quiet. Careful. Like I needed time to decide what I'd just seen.

Seeing a weight-loss drug behind her cotton pads felt like being lied to. A small confounding betrayal I'd needed her to be above.

I didn't speak to her for six months.

I'm on the same drug now.

And there's something I need to tell her before the symptom she's been hiding from me gets worse. I think it's already worse.

Let me back up.

My sister is forty-eight. I'm fifty-nine. We've been close in the way only sisters who survived the same childhood can be close. Three kids between us. One divorce survived (mine). Twenty-six years of Sunday dinners at our mother's table before our mother passed in 2022, and another three years of holding the family together at my kitchen table since.

She lives twelve miles from me in Eagle, Idaho. I live in Boise. I see her almost every week. Or I did, until that Saturday.

I was at her house helping wrap her daughter Maddie's tenth birthday gifts. We'd done this every year together since Maddie was born. She needed paper tape. She said it was in the bathroom drawer.

Behind a stack of cotton pads, in a folded CVS prescription bag, the Wegovy® label was visible through the plastic.

I stood there holding that drawer open for a long time. Then I closed it. I wrapped the gifts. I drank the coffee. I left two hours later without mentioning it.

I drove home and I told my husband Mike. Loudly. I told him she'd taken the easy way. I told him our mother would have been disappointed. I told him I thought she was stronger than that. I said the things you say at the kitchen counter when you're trying to make yourself feel better about a judgment you've just passed.

That night I didn't text her. She didn't text me.

Six months is a long time to not speak to your sister.

In April I missed my niece's birthday party. I lied to Mike about a migraine and stayed home.

In May our grandkids were on the same Little League team and I made sure I arrived after the first inning so we'd be sitting on opposite sides of the field.

In June I drafted a text four times and deleted it four times.

In July I unfollowed her on Instagram so I'd stop checking it.

In August I checked it anyway, on Mike's phone, while he was in the shower.

She'd lost more weight.

I ate the feeling for the rest of the month and into September.

In September my endocrinologist told me my A1C had climbed to 6.4.

She said, in plain English, that I was a year from an insulin pump if nothing changed.

She reminded me my mother had gone the insulin route at 52, and that I was already seven years past that.

She said the word Ozempic. She said Wegovy.

She said: "You have options your mother didn't have."

I drove home and I sat in the driveway for forty-five minutes before I went inside.

I thought about my sister.

I thought about what I'd said about her in my own kitchen seven months earlier.

I thought about my face in the bathroom mirror that night, saying "the real way."

I filled the Wegovy® prescription on a Monday.

I hid it in the glove compartment of my car until the Idaho afternoon sun moved off the windshield, because I didn't want it warming up in there. Then I brought it inside and put it in the back of the fridge.

I put it behind a jar of pickles Mike would never touch.

Then I stood in front of the open refrigerator for a long time looking at the pickle jar.

I had become the exact thing I had walked out of her bathroom for.

Same drug. Same shelf. Same jar.

I closed the fridge.

I lost 51 pounds in the next eight months.

I didn't tell anyone. Not Mike. Not my daughter Jenny in Portland. Not my son Tyler who lives ten minutes away. Especially not Diane.

I was coasting on the lie for a while.

I could take the drug and not have the conversation.

I could be a hypocrite in private.

Then at month three, I went six days without going to the bathroom.

Not painful at first. Just a slow, building bloat. I bought a tub of Metamucil at Albertsons and put it on the counter so Mike would think I was just being responsible about fiber.

Then the burps started.

You know the ones. The rotten-egg taste at the back of your throat. The kind that make the woman next to you on the elliptical at Boise Athletic Club move two machines down.

I cancelled book club. I cancelled lunch with my friend Karen. I told them I had a sinus thing.

By the end of month four I was waking up at three in the morning every single night.

Bone-on-bone burning low in my abdomen. Cramping that wouldn't move. I'd get up, go downstairs, take a Tylenol, sit at the kitchen table waiting for it to take the edge off, and stare at the back of the fridge where the Wegovy pen sat behind the pickle jar.

I never told Mike.

Because the day I told him out loud was the day I'd have to choose between the drug that was finally getting my A1C in range and admitting I'd hidden it from him for ten months.

I went to my GP at month four and a half.

She ran a panel. Iron, ferritin, magnesium, thyroid, B12, protein.

Everything came back normal.

"This is just how some people respond to rapid weight loss," she said. "Increase your fiber. Add a daily Miralax. Take a magnesium tablet at bedtime if it gets bad. It's going to settle. Give it three to six months."

I did exactly what she said.

Week 1-4: Metamucil twice a day. Choked down the wet cardboard. Result: marginal first week, plateau.

Week 5-8: Switched to Miralax every morning. Result: 30% better, then back to baseline.

Week 9-12: My GP wrote me a prescription for Citrucel. $94 for a 60-day supply.

No different than Miralax. I was now spending $94 every two months on what was essentially expensive fiber.

Week 13-16: Amazon "GLP-1 multivitamin" that promised "complete gut support." $42 with overnight Prime.

Marginal first week. Plateau by week three.

I spent over $360 in four months on supplements and prescription fiber and stomach acid blockers because the Tylenol I was taking every night had burned a hole in my stomach lining.

I still hadn't gone normally in five months.

And I was starting to notice something else.

Sometimes at the top of the stairs I'd feel a little flutter in my chest. Not pain. Not enough to mention. Just enough to make me stop and put my hand on the bannister for a second before I kept going.

I told myself it was the stairs. I was 59. The stairs were going to get harder.

Then my friend Karen called me in February and told me her sister-in-law's cardiologist had found atrial fibrillation in a woman who'd lost 60 pounds on Mounjaro® in nine months.

"Karen," I said. "What does atrial fibrillation feel like?"

"Sometimes nothing," she said. "Sometimes a little flutter in your chest at the top of the stairs."

I sat down on my couch and didn't say anything for a long time.

The next morning I made an appointment with my GP for a referral.

Six-week wait for cardiology.

While I waited, I went to refill my Wegovy® at the independent pharmacy on Bannock Street in downtown Boise. Coleman Pharmacy. I'd been going there for four years — small, two-pharmacist shop, owned by a woman named Dr. Sarah Coleman who'd been a hospital pharmacist at St. Luke's Boise for thirty-one years before opening her own place.

She knew my whole medication history. She knew my A1C numbers. She knew my mother had been her patient at St. Luke's.

When she handed me my prescription, she asked the question my GP never asked.

"How are you actually feeling, Carol?"

I told her. The bowel movements. The burps. The Tylenol. The Amazon multivitamin. The fluttering at the top of the stairs.

She set the prescription bag down very slowly on the counter and looked at me.

"Carol. Come to the back."

She walked me to a small consultation room where she did her medication-therapy reviews. Sat me down at a table. Then she opened a binder and turned to a page near the front.

"Can I tell you something I learned in thirty-one years filling prescriptions for every medication you can name?"

I nodded.

"Your GP told you the truth about your symptoms. But she told you only half of it. There's not one problem happening here. There are two. And almost no GP is addressing the second one because it doesn't show up in standard labs."

"I had standard labs. They were normal."

"I know. They almost always are."

She slid the binder across the table to me.

"Your medication — Wegovy®, Ozempic®, Mounjaro® — they slow gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That's the therapeutic effect. It's why your A1C dropped. It's also why food sits in your stomach long enough to start fermenting. Those are the sulfur burps. And it's why your intestinal motility slowed, which is the constipation. Your GP is treating those symptoms. She's not wrong about them. They're real, and with the right protocol they resolve."

"Okay."

"But here's what almost nobody is telling women on GLP-1s. While you've been losing weight, your body has been depleting its magnesium stores at three times the normal rate. Rapid fat loss triggers it. Reduced food intake compounds it. And the magnesium that goes first is the magnesium your body considers most disposable — which is not, unfortunately, the magnesium in your blood. It's the magnesium in your tissues. Your cardiac muscle. Your nerve endings. Your bone."

"But my magnesium test was normal."

"Carol. Less than one percent of your body's magnesium is in your blood. The blood test tells you what's in the bloodstream right now. It tells you almost nothing about what's in your heart muscle. Or your nerves. Or your bones. The body protects serum magnesium last and hardest, because if blood magnesium crashes, you die. So it strips the tissues first. The blood looks fine for months while the tissues quietly empty out."

I thought about the flutter at the top of the stairs.

She kept going.

"Magnesium is the cofactor for over six hundred enzymatic processes in your body. The two most magnesium-dependent tissues you have are your cardiac muscle and your neural tissue. When you deplete tissue magnesium fast — and a GLP-1 patient losing weight is depleting it fast — the cardiac muscle starts having trouble relaxing properly between contractions. That's how atrial fibrillation begins. Quietly. Intermittently. Before anyone catches it on an EKG."

"That's what's happening when I feel the flutter."

"I would bet on it. And here's the worst part. The fiber and the Miralax your GP gave you — those don't address it. The Amazon multivitamin you tried — that doesn't address it either. Most generic magnesium tablets are magnesium oxide, which your gut barely absorbs. The magnesium that actually reaches the tissue has to be a bioavailable form — citrate, glycinate, or a combination — at a therapeutic dose, paired with something that addresses the gastric emptying side."

"Why has nobody told me this?"

"Because the supplement industry has spent thirty years selling fiber to constipated people. The GLP-1 wave is brand new. Most companies are slapping 'GLP-1 SUPPORT' on existing multivitamin labels and charging double for the same thing they were selling in 2019. Ninety percent of what's on Amazon under that label is under-dosed magnesium with no real ginger and no thought to the actual mechanism."

"You've tested them?"

"Last year I sent fifteen of the most popular GLP-1-positioned supplements on Amazon to a third-party lab in Seattle. We did blind assays."

She turned the page in the binder.

"Brand A — labeled 250mg magnesium glycinate — actually contained 23mg of magnesium per dose. Ninety percent under-dosed."

"Brand B — labeled 200mg ginger root extract — was unstandardized commercial powder. No measurable gingerols. Useless."

"Brand C — labeled 500mg magnesium citrate — was magnesium oxide, which your body absorbs maybe 4% of."

"Brand D was contaminated with heavy metals at levels above the FDA's CFR-111 limits."

She paused.

"Exactly one product passed the assay. Magnesium delivered as labeled, in bioavailable citrate-glycinate form. Ginger root standardized to 5% gingerols. Methylcobalamin B12, not the cheap cyanocobalamin synthetic. Manufactured in a single FDA-registered facility in Ruston, Utah. Third-party tested every batch. No fillers."

She wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy® and went through what you're going through. She found a formulator who actually understood the dual mechanism. I recommend it to every GLP-1 patient who walks into this pharmacy now. I have no business relationship with the company. I just don't want to keep watching women like you end up in cardiology waiting rooms for something that was preventable."

I looked at the prescription pad. GLP-1 SOS™.

"And this fixes both problems?"

"If you start now, before the cardiac symptoms become a confirmed diagnosis — yes. Two capsules with dinner. Magnesium pulls water into your gut gently overnight and reaches the depleted tissue including the cardiac muscle. Ginger speeds gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation. B12 rebuilds the nerve and energy reserves. You should see regularity in three days. Sulfur burps usually resolve in 48 hours. The fluttering — if it really is early magnesium depletion — should settle within four to six weeks as the tissue stores rebuild."

"What about my cardiology appointment?"

"Keep it. Tell the cardiologist exactly what we just discussed. Ask her about intracellular magnesium testing if she's seeing rhythm signals. But start the supplement tonight, not after the appointment. Every week you wait is a week the tissue keeps depleting."

"How much is it?"

"$24.99 a month on subscription. Less than what you're already spending on Citrucel and Tylenol and the stomach acid blocker for the lining damage the Tylenol caused. And it has a 60-day money-back guarantee. If it doesn't work for you, you get every dollar back, no return required."

I ordered it from the parking lot.

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. I started to wonder if Dr. Coleman was wrong.

Day three, I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. Just normal. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward for a minute because I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

✅ 48 hours after my first dose: I had coffee with Karen at our usual spot. I waited for the sulfur burps. They didn't come.

✅ Week 2: I slept through the night without cramping. Eight hours straight for the first time since September.

✅ Week 3: I had energy at 3 PM. I weeded the entire front yard. I hadn't done that since the spring.

✅ Week 4: Mike and I went out for our anniversary at Chandlers downtown and I sat for two and a half hours and ate prime rib and never once thought about the bathroom.

✅ Week 5: I climbed the stairs at home and at the top, I waited. The flutter didn't come.

✅ Week 8: My A1C check came back at 5.7. Not 6.4. Not 5.9. Five point seven. My endocrinologist asked what I'd changed. I told her. She wrote it down.

Then I went to my cardiology appointment.

Saint Alphonsus on West Emerald.

I'd been doing fine for six weeks but I kept the appointment because Dr. Coleman had said to.

The cardiology waiting room is on the second floor. Soft fluorescent lighting. Vinyl chairs. People magazine. Botanical prints on the walls. I checked in and sat down with a clipboard.

Four chairs to my left, on the opposite side of the same row, was my sister.

Diane.

She was wearing an oversized cream cardigan that hung off her shoulders. She'd lost more weight since August — I could see it now even through the sweater. Her hair was in a low loose ponytail. She had a glucose monitor in her open canvas tote on the chair beside her, showing a reading I couldn't make out.

The cardigan was hiding loose skin under her arms. I knew that cardigan. She'd bought it the year our mother died because she needed something soft to wear to the visitation. She'd worn it almost every day for a month after.

She didn't see me.

I sat there with my clipboard in my lap for a long time without filling it out. I watched her.

She was staring at her hands.

She had her right hand pressed lightly against her sternum, the way you do when you're not in pain but you're waiting for the not-pain to turn into pain.

I knew that gesture. I'd been doing it on the stairs for five months.

Diane had been doing it longer.

She hadn't told me. We hadn't been speaking.

She hadn't told anyone, I would guess. Her husband John. Her son Tyler in college. Nobody.

Because the day she said it out loud was the day she'd have to admit, to the people she loved, that the drug she'd been hiding behind cotton pads was the same drug that had brought her to a cardiology waiting room on a Tuesday in February.

I sat there.

I almost got up. I almost crossed the four chairs. I almost said her name.

Then the receptionist called me. "Carol Hendricks?"

I stood up. I picked up my clipboard. I walked past her row. She still didn't look up.

I went into my appointment.

The cardiologist examined me, listened to my heart for a long time, ran the EKG. Then she sat across from me at her little desk and said: "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it. Your rhythm is fine. You're going to be fine."

I asked her about intracellular magnesium testing. She looked at me strangely and said it wasn't standard. But she said she had been seeing a noticeable uptick in rhythm complaints from GLP-1 patients in the last eight months and that if I was being proactive about it, I was probably saving her a future appointment.

I left her office. I walked back through the waiting room.

The chair where Diane had been sitting was empty.

I drove home, opened my laptop, and started writing.

If you're on a GLP-1 medication, or you're about to start one, or you're five months in and you're starting to feel a flutter at the top of the stairs, please understand what I didn't understand until a pharmacist drew me a diagram on the back of a prescription pad.

There are two problems, not one.

The first one — the constipation, the sulfur burps, the fatigue — your GP is treating. It will eventually slow. Maybe in six months. Maybe in a year. It is real and it is hard but it does, eventually, settle.

The second one — the silent tissue magnesium depletion — your GP isn't testing for and probably hasn't considered. It doesn't slow on its own. It doesn't resolve when your weight stabilizes. It is the one that puts women like Diane in the cardiology waiting room.

You're declining the trip to your daughter's wedding venue tour because you can't sit on the airplane for four hours without the bloating coming back.

You're skipping your grandson's first birthday because the cramping has been worse this week and you don't want to ruin the day.

You're hiding the Wegovy® behind the pickles because the day you admit you're still on it is the day Mike will ask why you haven't gotten off it yet, which is the question you don't have an answer to.

If you go once every 3 or 4 days no matter how much water you drink or how much fiber you choke down — and you keep getting told to "just give it time" — I want to tell you what finally made sense of all of it for me.

Because I watched my best friend live it. And once I understood what was actually going on, I'll be honest: I was angry. Not at any one person. Angry that the answer was this simple, and it took us almost two years to find it.

Let me tell you about Gail.

For the better part of two years, my best friend was miserable. Her constipation got so bad she'd go once every five or six days — not "a little backed up," but sitting in the bathroom for 45 minutes, straining, near tears, feeling like her body had simply stopped working.

Her stomach stayed bloated to the point that she looked six months pregnant after every meal. Everything in her closet had to be stretchy or loose, because by 3 PM her waistband was cutting into her.

And the fog. She'd sleep eight hours and wake up feeling like she'd been sedated. She'd lose the end of her own sentences. Her energy was gone by 2 PM every single day. She started to feel like she was going a little crazy, because nobody could tell her what was actually wrong.

It all started a few months after she began her shots.

So she did what you're supposed to do. She saw her doctor. A gastroenterologist. Thousands of dollars in appointments, bloodwork, a colonoscopy, stool tests — the whole nine yards. And every result came back "normal."

And the advice was always the same:

"Your bloodwork looks fine." "It's probably just IBS." "Drink more water." "Eat more fiber." "Have you tried Miralax?"

Here's the thing — none of that advice is wrong, exactly. For a typical gut, it's perfectly reasonable. It just wasn't built for what was actually happening to hers. And that's the part nobody connected for her.

They had her on Miralax, Metamucil, probiotics, magnesium — a rotating door of band-aids. The fiber powders made her more bloated. Months of money, restrictive diets, cutting out gluten and dairy. She couldn't enjoy a meal or leave the house without mapping the bathrooms. And nothing got better. It stayed the same or got worse.

I couldn't stand watching her do everything she was told and keep sinking. So I started reading. Late nights, medical journals, functional-medicine articles. And I finally found the piece no one had ever explained to her.

Here's what nobody tells you: your gut isn't supposed to need to be forced. It moves on its own — in waves. Peristalsis. The muscles squeeze in a rhythm and push everything along. That rhythm is what "regular" actually means. Not a flush. A rhythm.

And a GLP-1 slows that rhythm down. That's literally how the medication works — it slows your stomach so you stay full longer. The full feeling is the whole point. The gut grinding to a crawl is the side effect nobody warns you about.

So once the rhythm has stalled, drinking more water and eating more fiber doesn't fix it. You're just loading more cargo onto a train that isn't moving. And laxatives? They shove water past the stall. None of them restart the rhythm.

It's like a train yard where every car is loaded and ready — but no signal ever goes out to move them. The cars are fine. The track is fine. Nothing leaves the yard.

That's why you can drink gallons of water, eat pounds of fiber, and still go once every four days. The raw materials are all there. The gut just isn't getting the push to move them.

And here's what actually helps a slowed-down gut — and not one of them is a laxative:

Magnesium, the citrate form, draws in a little water gently and relaxes the gut wall. It works with a slow system instead of blasting it.

Ginger — and this is the one almost no one talks about — is a clinically-studied prokinetic. It supports the stomach emptying that a GLP-1 slows down. It works at the source, not just the exit.

The right gut bacteria — a real multi-strain probiotic to support the flora that keep things moving and calm the fermentation behind the bloating and the sulfur burps. (Eating 60% less on a GLP-1 quietly starves them.)

This isn't fringe. Ginger has been studied for gastric motility for years. Magnesium is one of the most-studied minerals there is for regularity. It's just not the one-size advice you get in a ten-minute appointment. It's a different problem, so it needs a different fix.

Gail finally found a functional medicine doctor who actually looked deeper — and told her almost word-for-word what I'd been reading. Her gut had slowed down. Laxatives were never going to restart it. She needed to gently support the motility and rebuild her flora, or the constipation would keep coming back. For the first time in two years, someone explained why nothing had worked.

But finding the right combination — the right doses, the right forms — was a nightmare. Cheap oxide magnesium you barely absorb. Ginger that's just ground spice with no standardized active.
